unit.unitOverview: Level 1 gave you the past simple, which puts events in a line. This unit gives you the two forms that break the line: the past continuous, which sets a scene, and the past perfect, which reaches back behind the story you are telling. Together they let you narrate something complicated without telling it strictly in order. It ends with two witness statements about the same two minutes.

visual.lectureScript:
In Level 1 Unit 14 you learned the past simple, and with it you can tell any story as a sequence. I arrived. I checked it. I went home. That works, and it produces a list.
This unit adds the two forms that let you do something better than a list.
First pattern: the past continuous.
The form is was or were plus the -ing form. I was waiting. They were working.
And its job is background. It describes something that was already going on when something else happened.
I was waiting on the platform when the announcement came.
The waiting is the setting. The announcement is the event. The waiting started before it and probably continued after it.
That is why the past continuous is how English opens a narrative. It was raining. People were queuing outside. Nobody was expecting it. None of those are events. They are the situation the events happen in.
Three words go with it, and they behave differently.
When usually introduces the event — the shorter thing, in the past simple. I was waiting when it happened.
While usually introduces the background — the longer thing, in the past continuous. While I was waiting, it happened.
So when and while point in opposite directions, and that is worth holding: when takes the event, while takes the background.
Until marks the end of the background. I was waiting until they called my name. The waiting stopped at that point.
Second pattern, and it only compares. Past simple against past continuous.
I am putting this in its own card because the choice is what makes narration sound natural, and it is not really about grammar — it is about what you are treating as background and what you are treating as an event.
The rule: past simple for the events, past continuous for the situation they happen in.
Watch what changes.
When I arrived, she made a call. Two events, one after the other. She started the call after I got there.
When I arrived, she was making a call. One background, one event. The call was already happening.
Same words apart from the verb form, and two different scenes.
And one more contrast worth having.
I read the report. Finished — you know what it said.
I was reading the report. Ongoing, and you may not have finished. Which is why I was reading it when you called is a normal sentence and I read it when you called is odd.
Third pattern: the past perfect. Had plus the past participle.
This is the tense for something that happened before the past you are already talking about.
When I arrived, she had already left.
Two past events. The leaving came first, the arriving came second, and the past perfect is what tells you the order.
This matters because English narration does not have to be chronological. You can tell things out of order, and the past perfect is what stops the reader getting lost.
I got to the office at nine. The door was open, which was unusual. Somebody had been in during the night.
That last sentence is earlier than everything before it, and had been in is what signals that.
Now the thing that saves you effort: you do not need the past perfect when the order is already clear.
I finished the report and sent it. Obviously in that order. I had finished the report and then I sent it is correct and unnecessarily heavy.
Use the past perfect when the order is not obvious, or when you are deliberately going backwards. Otherwise the past simple is fine and sounds better.
There is a continuous version too, and it does the job you would expect. I had been waiting for an hour when they finally called me. The waiting went on, and it finished before the calling.
Fourth pattern: participle clauses. This is the one that will change how your writing looks.
A participle clause is a way of joining two things about the same subject without a conjunction.
Having finished the report, I went home.
That means: after I had finished the report, I went home. Two clauses, one subject, and the first has been compressed into two words.
There are two kinds.
The -ing kind, for something happening at the same time or immediately connected. Walking home, I realised I had left my keys. Turning the corner, I saw the queue.
The having kind, for something completed before. Having finished the report, I went home. Having checked it twice, she signed it.
And there is one rule you must not break, because breaking it produces sentences that are unintentionally absurd.
The subject of the participle clause has to be the subject of the main clause.
Walking home, I saw the fire. Correct — I was walking and I saw.
Walking home, the fire was visible. Wrong — that says the fire was walking home.
This error is called a dangling participle and it is very common, including in professional writing. The test takes a second: ask who is doing the -ing, and check that it is the subject of the sentence that follows.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Background and Event
readings.passageScript:
The past simple puts events in a line. I arrived, I checked it, I went home. That is a list, and for a simple story a list is enough.
The past continuous does something a list cannot. It sets a scene.
I was waiting on the platform when the announcement came.
The waiting is the setting. It started before the announcement and probably continued after it. The announcement is the event that happens inside the setting.
This is why English opens narratives in the past continuous. It was raining. People were queuing outside. Nobody was expecting it. None of those are events — they are the situation that events will happen in.
Three words go with this and they behave differently, which is where errors happen.
When usually introduces the event, in the past simple. I was waiting when it happened.
While usually introduces the background, in the past continuous. While I was waiting, it happened.
So when and while point in opposite directions. When takes the shorter thing; while takes the longer one.
Until marks where the background stops. I was waiting until they called my name.
Now the comparison that decides how natural your narration sounds, and it is not really a grammar choice.
When I arrived, she made a call.
When I arrived, she was making a call.
The first has two events in sequence: I got there, then she started the call. The second has a background and an event: the call was already going on when I walked in.
Same words apart from the verb form, and two completely different scenes.
So the question is never which tense is correct. It is which thing you are treating as the setting and which as the thing that happened. Both sentences above are correct English, and they describe different afternoons.

readings.title: Going Backwards Without Getting Lost
readings.passageScript:
Stories are rarely told in the order things happened, and English has a tense whose whole job is to let you go backwards safely.
The past perfect — had plus the past participle — marks something as earlier than the past you are already in.
I got to the office at nine. The door was open, which was unusual. Somebody had been in during the night.
That last event is the earliest of the three and it is told last. Had been in is what tells the reader so, and without it they would assume somebody came in after you arrived.
This is the practical value of the tense. It is not decoration and it is not formality. It is the thing that lets you introduce information out of order without confusing anybody.
Now the part that saves you effort, and that most courses underplay.
You do not need it when the order is already obvious.
I finished the report and sent it. Nobody could read that in the wrong order. Writing I had finished the report and then I sent it is correct and unnecessarily heavy.
The past perfect earns its place when the order is not obvious, or when you are deliberately reaching back. Everywhere else the past simple is better.
A useful check: if you could remove the had and the sentence would still be understood in the same order, remove it.
There is a continuous version, and it does exactly what you would expect. I had been waiting for an hour when they finally called me. The waiting was going on for a period, and it ended before the calling.
One last thing about narration generally. Once you have both these tenses, you can tell a two-minute incident in whatever order makes it clearest — set the scene in the continuous, give the events in the simple, and reach back with the perfect wherever the reader needs to know that something had already happened. Most real accounts of anything complicated do exactly that, and the ones that are hard to follow are usually the ones told strictly in order.

readings.title: Two Minutes, Two Accounts
readings.setting: Two statements about the same incident in a warehouse, taken the same afternoon.
readings.passageScript:
STATEMENT ONE - J. Marsh

  I was checking the loading sheet in Bay
  3 when I heard something fall in Bay 2.

  I did not see it happen. By the time I
  got there the stack had already come
  down and two people were standing at
  the edge of it.

  Somebody had moved the trolley before I
  arrived - it was about a metre from
  where it normally sits. I do not know
  who moved it.

  Having checked that nobody was hurt, I
  went to find the supervisor.

-----------------------------------------

  STATEMENT TWO - A. Bello

  I was walking through Bay 2 towards the
  side door. The stack collapsed as I was
  passing it. I was about three metres
  away.

  I had noticed earlier that morning that
  it was leaning, and I had mentioned it
  to the shift manager. Nothing had been
  done.

  I did not move the trolley. It was
  already where it was when I came
  through.

  Turning round, I saw J. Marsh arriving
  from Bay 3. That was maybe ten seconds
  afterwards.

grammar.title: The past continuous, and when, while, until
grammar.explanation: Was or were plus the -ing form. Its job is background — the situation that was already going on when something else happened.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FORM: was / were + -ING
  I was waiting.   They were working.

ITS JOB IS BACKGROUND
  I was waiting on the platform when the
  announcement came.
     waiting = the setting
     announcement = the event

HOW NARRATIVES OPEN
  It was raining. People were queuing
  outside. Nobody was expecting it.
  ^ none of these are events.

WHEN, WHILE, UNTIL
  WHEN  -> the EVENT (past simple)
     I was waiting when it happened.
  WHILE -> the BACKGROUND (continuous)
     While I was waiting, it happened.
  UNTIL -> where the background STOPS
     I was waiting until they called me.

  when and while point OPPOSITE ways.
  when takes the shorter thing.
  while takes the longer one.

STATE VERBS RESIST IT
  I knew, I was, I owned
  NOT I was knowing (see Unit 3)
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that you were on the platform for a while, and during that time an announcement was made.
1. Decide which is background and which is event. The waiting is longer, so it is background. The announcement is shorter, so it is the event.
2. Background takes the past continuous: I was waiting on the platform.
3. The event takes the past simple: the announcement came.
4. Now join them. Since when introduces the event, put when in front of the announcement: I was waiting on the platform when the announcement came.
5. Or turn it round using while, which introduces the background: While I was waiting on the platform, the announcement came.
Both are correct and they say the same thing. What you cannot do is swap them — while the announcement came is wrong, because the announcement is not a background.
Check by length: the longer action always goes with while, and the shorter with when.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting while with the short event — while the announcement came, I was waiting. It is the wrong way round, and the test is which action lasted longer. The other error is using the past continuous with state verbs — I was knowing, I was owning — which is the same restriction as the present continuous in Unit 3.
grammar.memoryTip: While takes the long one. When takes the short one.
grammar.practice:
Complete each with the past continuous or past simple.
1. I ____ (wait) on the platform when the announcement ____ (come).
2. While I ____ (check) the sheet, something ____ (fall).
3. The stack ____ (collapse) while nobody ____ (watch).
4. I ____ (wait) until they ____ (call) my name.
5. She ____ (make) a call when I ____ (arrive). (the call was already going on)
6. She ____ (make) a call when I ____ (arrive). (she started it after I got there)
grammar.answerKey:
1. was waiting / came
2. was checking / fell
3. collapsed / was watching
4. was waiting / called
5. was making / arrived
6. made / arrived
Numbers 5 and 6 are the same words with different verb forms and different meanings. In 5 the call is the background; in 6 it is the second of two events.
In number 3 the order is reversed — the event comes first and while introduces the background afterwards. That is normal and the pairing still holds.
Number 4 uses until, which ends the background rather than interrupting it.

grammar.title: Past simple versus past continuous
grammar.explanation: This card only compares. The past simple is Level 1 Unit 14 and the past continuous is card 1 of this unit — nothing here is new. What is new is choosing, and the choice is about what you treat as background.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE PRINCIPLE
  past simple    -> the EVENTS
  past continuous -> the SITUATION they
                     happen in

WATCH WHAT CHANGES
  When I arrived, she made a call.
     two events in sequence.
     She started the call AFTER I got there.

  When I arrived, she was making a call.
     background + event.
     The call was ALREADY happening.

  Same words. Different afternoons.

FINISHED OR NOT
  I read the report.
     finished. You know what it said.
  I was reading the report.
     ongoing. You may not have finished.

  which is why:
     "I was reading it when you called"
     is normal, and
     "I read it when you called" is odd.

THE QUESTION IS NEVER WHICH IS CORRECT
  Both are correct English.
  Ask: which thing is the SETTING?
grammar.workedExample:
You walk into an office and somebody is already on the phone.
1. Which is the setting? The call — it was going on before you arrived and continued afterwards.
2. Setting takes the continuous: she was making a call.
3. Your arrival is the event: when I arrived.
4. Result: When I arrived, she was making a call.
Now the other situation. You walk in, and then she picks up the phone.
1. Now there is no background. Two things happened, one after the other.
2. Both are events, so both take the past simple.
3. Result: When I arrived, she made a call.
Neither sentence is more correct than the other. They describe different things, and choosing wrongly does not produce an error — it produces an accurate description of an afternoon that did not happen.
That is why this is a comparison card rather than a rule card. There is nothing to get right; there is something to decide.
grammar.commonMistake: Treating this as a correctness question and looking for the right answer. Both forms are always available and they mean different things. The practical error that follows is narrating everything in the past simple, which produces a list where the reader cannot tell what was already going on and what interrupted it.
grammar.memoryTip: Not which is correct. Which one is the setting.
grammar.practice:
For each pair, say what changes between the two versions.
1. When I arrived, she made a call. / When I arrived, she was making a call.
2. I read the report. / I was reading the report.
3. It rained. / It was raining.
4. He worked in the warehouse. / He was working in the warehouse.
5. The alarm sounded. / The alarm was sounding.
6. Now write one pair of your own and explain the difference.
grammar.answerKey:
1. First: she started the call after I got there. Second: the call was already going on.
2. First: finished, and you know what it said. Second: ongoing, and you may not have finished.
3. First: an event — it rained at some point. Second: a background — it was raining while something else happened.
4. First: a fact about a period of his life. Second: a temporary situation, or the setting for something else.
5. First: it went off at a moment. Second: it was already going off, and something happened during it.
6. Yours will vary. Check it has the same words and only the verb form differs.
Number 4 is the subtlest. He worked in the warehouse states his job; he was working in the warehouse suggests either a temporary arrangement or that this is the setting for what comes next.
In none of the six is one version wrong. Each pair describes two different situations.

grammar.title: The past perfect
grammar.explanation: Had plus the past participle. It marks something as earlier than the past you are already talking about, which is what lets you tell a story out of order.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FORM: HAD + PAST PARTICIPLE
  had left, had seen, had been,
  had already gone
  ^ had never changes for person.

ITS JOB: an EARLIER past
  When I arrived, she had already left.
     leaving came first.
     arriving came second.

WHY IT MATTERS
  it lets you go BACKWARDS safely.

  "I got to the office at nine. The door
   was open. Somebody HAD BEEN IN during
   the night."
  ^ earliest event, told last.

DO NOT USE IT WHEN THE ORDER IS OBVIOUS
  I finished the report and sent it.
  ^ nobody could read that backwards.
  "I had finished... and then I sent it"
  is correct and heavy.

THE CHECK
  remove the HAD. Is the order still
  clear? Then leave it out.

CONTINUOUS VERSION
  I had been waiting for an hour when
  they finally called me.
grammar.workedExample:
You arrived at nine and found the door open, and you later worked out that somebody had come in overnight.
1. Order the events. Somebody came in — first. You arrived — second. You noticed the door — third.
2. You want to tell it in the order you experienced it, which puts the earliest event last.
3. So the earliest one needs marking: had been in.
4. Result: I got to the office at nine. The door was open, which was unusual. Somebody had been in during the night.
5. Check what happens without it: somebody was in during the night reads as though it happened after you arrived, which is not what you mean.
Now one that does not need it. I finished the report and sent it.
1. Apply the check: remove any had. Is the order clear? Yes — you cannot send a report you have not finished.
2. So no past perfect. I had finished the report and then I sent it is correct and heavier than it needs to be.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the past perfect for everything that happened in the past, which makes narration slow and formal without adding information. The other error is the participle: had went, had saw, had took. The past perfect takes the third form — had gone, had seen, had taken — which is the same column as the passive in Unit 10 and the present perfect in Unit 3.
grammar.memoryTip: Only when the order is not obvious. Remove the had and see.
grammar.practice:
Write the past perfect where it is needed, and the past simple where it is not.
1. When I arrived, she ____ (already leave).
2. I ____ (finish) the report and ____ (send) it.
3. The stack ____ (already come) down by the time I got there.
4. Somebody ____ (move) the trolley before I arrived.
5. I ____ (notice) it that morning and ____ (mention) it to the manager.
6. I ____ (wait) for an hour when they finally called me.
grammar.answerKey:
1. had already left
2. finished / sent — the order is obvious, so no past perfect
3. had already come
4. had moved
5. had noticed / had mentioned — or noticed / mentioned, if you have already established that this was earlier
6. had been waiting
Number 2 is the one that tests the check. Nobody could misread finished and sent, so the past perfect would only add weight.
Numbers 1, 3 and 4 all contain a word that signals an earlier event — already, by the time, before — and those are exactly the contexts where the past perfect earns its place.
Number 6 is the continuous version, and it says the waiting went on for a period and ended when they called.

grammar.title: Participle clauses
grammar.explanation: A way of joining two things about the same subject without a conjunction. It compresses a whole clause into two words, and it has one rule you cannot break.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TWO KINDS

  -ING - same time, or immediately linked
     Walking home, I realised I had left
       my keys.
     Turning the corner, I saw the queue.
     = as I walked home / as I turned

  HAVING + PARTICIPLE - completed BEFORE
     Having finished the report, I went home.
     Having checked it twice, she signed it.
     = after I had finished / after she had
       checked

THE RULE YOU CANNOT BREAK
  the subject of the participle clause
  MUST be the subject of the main clause.

  Walking home, I saw the fire.      OK
     (I was walking, I saw)
  Walking home, the fire was visible. X
     (this says the FIRE was walking home)

  This is a DANGLING PARTICIPLE and it is
  very common, including in professional
  writing.

THE TEST
  ask who is doing the -ing.
  Check it is the subject of what follows.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say: after you had checked that nobody was hurt, you went to find the supervisor.
1. Is the earlier action completed before the second? Yes.
2. Completed before takes having plus the participle: having checked.
3. Add the rest of that clause: having checked that nobody was hurt.
4. Now the main clause, and it must have the same subject: I went to find the supervisor.
5. Result: Having checked that nobody was hurt, I went to find the supervisor.
6. Apply the test: who did the checking? I did. Who went? I did. Same subject, so it holds.
Now one that fails. Walking home, the fire was visible.
1. Who is doing the walking? The sentence does not say — the only subject available is the fire.
2. So it reads as the fire walking home.
3. Fix it by supplying the right subject: Walking home, I could see the fire.
The test takes a second and it catches every dangling participle.
grammar.commonMistake: The dangling participle — a participle clause whose subject is not the subject of the main clause. Having checked the loading, the trolley was moved says the trolley did the checking. It is extremely common and it is usually invisible to the writer, because they know who they meant. The other error is using -ing for something completed well before, where having is needed.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask who is doing the -ing. It must be the subject of the main clause.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each pair as one sentence with a participle clause.
1. I was walking home. I realised I had left my keys.
2. I had finished the report. I went home.
3. She had checked it twice. She signed it.
4. I turned round. I saw him arriving.
5. He had not been told. He carried on working.
6. Now correct this: Having checked the loading, the trolley was moved.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Walking home, I realised I had left my keys.
2. Having finished the report, I went home.
3. Having checked it twice, she signed it.
4. Turning round, I saw him arriving.
5. Not having been told, he carried on working.
6. Having checked the loading, I moved the trolley. — or: Having checked the loading, the supervisor moved the trolley.
Numbers 1 and 4 use -ing, because the two actions are simultaneous or immediately linked. Numbers 2, 3 and 5 use having, because the first action was completed before the second.
Number 5 shows the negative: not goes before having.
Number 6 was a dangling participle — the original says the trolley checked the loading. The fix is to supply the subject who actually did the checking, and both versions above work.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 6 Unit 7; Grade 7 Unit 8; Grade 8 Unit 7
writing.title: Writing 1 — An incident, out of order
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write an account of something that happened to you, real or invented, lasting no more than a few minutes.
Twelve to sixteen sentences.
Open with at least two sentences of past continuous setting the scene.
Give the events in the past simple.
Use the past perfect at least three times, and at least once to introduce information the reader did not have.
Use at least two participle clauses, one with -ing and one with having.
Then underline every past perfect and write beside it what it reaches back to.
writing.modelText:
It was raining and the yard was already flooding at the low end. Two of us were loading the last pallets and nobody else was outside.
I heard the gate before I saw anything. It slammed twice, which it does in wind, so I did not look up.
The second time, something else moved. The stack at the end of the row leaned about a foot and stopped.
We both froze. Then Dami shouted and we went towards it, which was probably wrong.
By the time we reached it, the top three cases had already come down on the far side. Nobody was underneath, and I remember being surprised rather than relieved.
Somebody had loaded that stack above the line, and I had noticed it the previous evening. I had said nothing, because it was not my bay and it had been like that for two days.
Having checked that we were both all right, I went to find the supervisor. Walking back across the yard, I worked out what I was going to say and then said something different.
The whole thing lasted about ninety seconds.

had already come down — before we reached it.
had loaded — before the previous evening.
had noticed — the previous evening, before everything above.
had been like that — before the previous evening, and continuing.
writing.successCriteria: At least two past continuous sentences setting the scene; events in the past simple; at least three past perfects, each underlined with what it reaches back to; at least one past perfect introducing new information; two participle clauses, one -ing and one having; no dangling participle
writing.support: Write the events in strict order first, as a plain list. Then decide which ones the reader should meet out of order, and those are the ones that become past perfects. Doing it in that order stops you using the tense by feel.
writing.extension: Remove every past perfect and read it again. Which sentences now read in the wrong order? Those were the ones that needed it, and any that still read correctly did not.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Two accounts of one event
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write two witness statements about the same short incident, from two people who saw different parts of it.
Each must be eight to twelve sentences.
Each must open in the past continuous.
Each must use the past perfect at least twice.
Each must contain at least one participle clause.
The two must agree on almost everything and disagree on exactly one fact, and neither statement may be able to settle it.
Then write two lines: what they disagree about, and why neither can resolve it.
writing.modelText:
STATEMENT ONE — R. Adeyemi
I was working on the till when I heard the shelving go. I did not see it fall.
By the time I got round the end of the aisle, the stock was already on the floor and one customer was standing about two metres back.
There was nobody else in that aisle. I had walked through it about ten minutes earlier and everything had been upright then.
The customer said she had not touched anything. I had no reason to doubt her.
Having checked that she was not hurt, I closed the aisle and rang the duty manager.
The trolley that is normally at the end of that aisle was not there. I do not know where it had gone.

STATEMENT TWO — customer, name withheld
I was looking at the top shelf when the whole unit moved. I was not touching it.
I had moved a trolley out of the way about a minute before, because it was blocking the aisle. I put it at the far end.
The unit leaned and then the top two shelves emptied. It took about three seconds.
Turning to get out of the way, I saw a member of staff coming round the corner almost immediately.
I had not seen anybody else in the aisle at any point.

1. They disagree about the trolley. Adeyemi says it was missing from its usual place and does not know where it had gone; the customer says she moved it a minute before and put it at the far end. Adeyemi does not know that.
2. Neither can settle it because Adeyemi was at the till and did not see the trolley moved, and the customer does not know where it normally sits, so she cannot know that moving it was unusual. Both accounts are honest and neither contains the information the other needs.
writing.expectedLength: Two statements of eight to twelve sentences
writing.successCriteria: Both open in the past continuous; both use the past perfect at least twice; both contain a participle clause with no dangling subject; the two agree on almost everything and disagree on exactly one fact; neither can settle the disagreement; two lines identifying the disagreement and explaining why it is unresolvable
writing.support: Decide the single disagreement before you write either statement, and decide what each witness could not have seen. The disagreement has to come from a genuine gap in what each one witnessed, not from either of them being wrong.
writing.extension: Write a third statement from somebody who saw the one thing that would settle it. How much shorter is it than the other two?

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two statements
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the two statements in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What was each witness doing when the stack fell, and how does the grammar tell you?
2. Find three past perfects and say what each reaches back to.
3. What do the two statements disagree about, and can either settle it?
4. Find the participle clause in each statement and write out what it means in full.
5. Put every event mentioned in both statements into the order in which it actually happened.
writing.modelText:
1. Marsh was checking the loading sheet in Bay 3; Bello was walking through Bay 2. Both are past continuous, which marks them as the ongoing situation rather than as events, so both were already under way when the stack fell.
2. The stack had already come down — before Marsh arrived in Bay 2. Somebody had moved the trolley — before Marsh arrived. Bello had noticed the stack was leaning and had mentioned it — earlier that morning, before everything else in either account. And nothing had been done — between the mention and the collapse.
3. The trolley. Marsh says somebody had moved it before he arrived, because it was a metre from where it normally sits; Bello says it was already where it was when she came through and that she did not move it. Neither can settle it: Marsh did not see the trolley before he arrived, and Bello does not say where it normally sits, so she may not know it had moved.
4. Marsh: Having checked that nobody was hurt, I went to find the supervisor — after I had checked that nobody was hurt, I went to find the supervisor. Bello: Turning round, I saw J. Marsh arriving — as I turned round, I saw him arriving.
5. Bello noticed the stack was leaning that morning. Bello mentioned it to the shift manager. Nothing was done. At some point the trolley moved, or did not. Marsh began checking the loading sheet in Bay 3; Bello began walking through Bay 2. The stack collapsed as Bello was passing. Marsh heard it and came from Bay 3, arriving about ten seconds later. Bello turned round and saw him. Marsh saw two people at the edge of the stack. Marsh checked nobody was hurt and went for the supervisor.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 explains the tense choice rather than only reporting the content; answer 3 explains why neither statement can resolve it; answer 5 places every event including the disputed trolley in a defensible order
writing.support: For question 5, write each event on its own line before ordering them. The past perfects tell you which ones belong earlier, and that is what the tense is for.
writing.extension: Which single piece of missing information would resolve the trolley question, and who would have had to be present to supply it?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. While the announcement came, I was waiting.
2. I was waiting while the announcement came.
3. I was knowing the answer.
4. When I arrived, she was make a call.
5. When I arrived, she made a call. (the call was already going on)
6. When I arrived, she had already leave.
7. I had finished the report and then I had sent it.
8. I had finish the report before I left.
9. Walking home, the fire was visible.
10. Having checked the loading, the trolley was moved.
11. Having walking home, I realised I had left my keys.
12. I was waiting for an hour when they finally called me. (you want to stress the whole hour)
writing.modelText:
1. While I was waiting, the announcement came. (Pattern 1 — while takes the background)
2. I was waiting when the announcement came. (Pattern 1 — when takes the event)
3. I knew the answer. (Pattern 1 — state verbs resist the continuous)
4. When I arrived, she was making a call. (Pattern 1 — the continuous needs the -ing form)
5. When I arrived, she was making a call. (Pattern 2 — an ongoing background takes the continuous)
6. When I arrived, she had already left. (Pattern 3 — the past perfect takes the third form)
7. I finished the report and sent it. (Pattern 3 — the order is obvious, so no past perfect)
8. I had finished the report before I left. (Pattern 3 — had takes the participle, not the plain verb)
9. Walking home, I could see the fire. (Pattern 4 — dangling participle; the fire was not walking)
10. Having checked the loading, I moved the trolley. (Pattern 4 — dangling participle; the trolley did not check)
11. Walking home, I realised I had left my keys. (Pattern 4 — -ing for a simultaneous action, not having)
12. I had been waiting for an hour when they finally called me. (Pattern 3 — the past perfect continuous)
Extension note: 7 could also keep one past perfect if the order genuinely needed marking, but here it does not.
writing.successCriteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 1 and 2 corrected in opposite directions; numbers 9 and 10 fixed by supplying the right subject rather than by repunctuating

activities.title: Practice 1 — Background or event
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the past simple or past continuous.
1. I ____ (wait) on the platform when the announcement ____ (come).
2. While I ____ (check) the sheet, something ____ (fall).
3. The stack ____ (collapse) while nobody ____ (watch).
4. I ____ (wait) until they ____ (call) my name.
5. She ____ (make) a call when I ____ (arrive). (already going on)
6. She ____ (make) a call when I ____ (arrive). (started afterwards)
7. It ____ (rain) and the yard ____ (flood) at the low end.
8. Two of us ____ (load) pallets when the gate ____ (slam).
9. I ____ (glance) at the board while I ____ (wait).
10. He ____ (stand) at the edge when it ____ (happen).
11. The alarm ____ (sound) while we ____ (work).
12. Nobody ____ (expect) it. (a background state)
activities.answerSummary:
1. was waiting / came  2. was checking / fell  3. collapsed / was watching  4. was waiting / called  5. was making / arrived  6. made / arrived  7. was raining / was flooding  8. were loading / slammed  9. glanced / was waiting  10. was standing / happened  11. sounded / were working  12. was expecting
Numbers 5 and 6 are identical apart from the verb form and describe different situations. Neither is wrong.
In every sentence, while took the longer action and when took the shorter one — check yours against that.
Number 9 is worth noticing: glanced is short and takes the past simple even though it is the first-mentioned action. Position in the sentence does not decide it; length does.

activities.title: Practice 2 — What changes?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
For each pair, write one line saying what changes between the two versions.
1. When I arrived, she made a call. / When I arrived, she was making a call.
2. I read the report. / I was reading the report.
3. It rained. / It was raining.
4. He worked in the warehouse. / He was working in the warehouse.
5. The alarm sounded. / The alarm was sounding.
6. She lived there for a year. / She was living there for a year.
7. I spoke to him. / I was speaking to him.
8. They loaded the pallets. / They were loading the pallets.
9. The door slammed. / The door was slamming.
10. I waited. / I was waiting.
11. She checked it. / She was checking it.
12. Nobody noticed. / Nobody was noticing.
activities.answerSummary:
1. First: she started the call after I got there. Second: it was already going on.
2. First: finished. Second: ongoing, and possibly unfinished.
3. First: an event. Second: a background for something else.
4. First: a fact about his job. Second: temporary, or the setting for what follows.
5. First: it went off at a moment. Second: it was already going off.
6. First: a completed period. Second: temporary, and it invites a but.
7. First: a completed exchange. Second: it was interrupted or is the setting.
8. First: they finished. Second: they were part-way through.
9. First: once. Second: repeatedly, in the wind.
10. First: the waiting is treated as an event. Second: it is the background.
11. First: she completed the check. Second: she was part-way through.
12. First: nobody noticed at all. Second: sounds odd — notice is close to a state verb and resists the continuous.
Number 9 shows something the card does not: with a repeatable action, the continuous can suggest repetition rather than duration.
Number 12 is the one that does not work well in both forms, and that is the state-verb restriction from card 1.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Does it need the past perfect?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the correct form, and mark NEEDED or NOT NEEDED for the past perfect.
1. When I arrived, she ____ (already leave).
2. I ____ (finish) the report and ____ (send) it.
3. The stack ____ (already come) down by the time I got there.
4. Somebody ____ (move) the trolley before I arrived.
5. I ____ (notice) it that morning and ____ (mention) it.
6. I ____ (wait) for an hour when they finally called me.
7. I got up, ____ (have) breakfast and ____ (leave).
8. The door was open. Somebody ____ (be) in during the night.
9. She ____ (check) it twice and then ____ (sign) it.
10. By the time the engineer came, the fault ____ (disappear).
11. He ____ (not be) told, so he carried on working.
12. I ____ (open) the door and ____ (go) in.
activities.answerSummary:
1. had already left — NEEDED (already signals an earlier past)
2. finished / sent — NOT NEEDED (the order is obvious)
3. had already come — NEEDED (by the time)
4. had moved — NEEDED (before I arrived, and the reader meets it later)
5. had noticed / had mentioned — NEEDED if this is being introduced as earlier background; NOT NEEDED if the sequence is already established
6. had been waiting — NEEDED, and continuous
7. had / left — NOT NEEDED (a plain sequence)
8. had been — NEEDED (this is the earliest event and it is told last)
9. checked / signed — NOT NEEDED (obvious order)
10. had disappeared — NEEDED (by the time)
11. had not been told — NEEDED (it explains something that came after)
12. opened / went — NOT NEEDED
The NEEDED ones cluster around three signals: already, by the time, and before. Where none of those appears and the order is obvious, the past simple is better.
Number 5 has two defensible answers, which is worth noticing — the tense depends on how you have framed the paragraph, not only on the events.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Compress into a participle clause
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Join each pair into one sentence with a participle clause. Then check who is doing the -ing.
1. I was walking home. I realised I had left my keys.
2. I had finished the report. I went home.
3. She had checked it twice. She signed it.
4. I turned round. I saw him arriving.
5. He had not been told. He carried on working.
6. She was standing at the edge. She saw the whole thing.
7. I had read the file. I understood the problem.
8. They were waiting for the part. They started something else.
9. She had already apologised. She said nothing further.
10. I opened the door. I noticed the smell.
11. He had worked there for a decade. He knew everybody.
12. Now fix this: Having checked the loading, the trolley was moved.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Walking home, I realised I had left my keys.
2. Having finished the report, I went home.
3. Having checked it twice, she signed it.
4. Turning round, I saw him arriving.
5. Not having been told, he carried on working.
6. Standing at the edge, she saw the whole thing.
7. Having read the file, I understood the problem.
8. Waiting for the part, they started something else.
9. Having already apologised, she said nothing further.
10. Opening the door, I noticed the smell.
11. Having worked there for a decade, he knew everybody.
12. Having checked the loading, I moved the trolley. (or: the supervisor moved the trolley)
The -ing versions — 1, 4, 6, 8, 10 — are all simultaneous or immediately linked. The having versions — 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 — are all completed before the main clause.
Number 5 puts not before having, which is the standard position for the negative.
Number 12 was a dangling participle: the original says the trolley did the checking. Every one of your answers should survive the test — ask who is doing the -ing, and check it is the subject of what follows.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Narrate something real
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write an account of something that happened this week, in twelve sentences.
Set the scene in the past continuous.
Use the past perfect wherever the reader needs to know something happened earlier.
Then give it to somebody, or leave it a day and read it as a stranger.
Write three lines: where they were confused, whether any past perfect was unnecessary, and whether any was missing.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your account.
What most people find: at least one past perfect is unnecessary, and it is usually in the first half. Learners who have just learned the tense apply it to the first thing that happened in the account, when the past simple would do — the reader has no earlier past to be confused about yet.
The second finding is the opposite and it is more useful. There is often one place where a past perfect is missing, and it is where the writer introduced something the reader had not been told about. That is exactly where the tense earns its place, and it is the hardest spot to notice yourself because you already knew the information.
Giving it to somebody else finds that spot faster than anything else.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find the dangling participle
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, look for participle clauses in real writing — reports, news, instructions, official letters.
Copy out six exactly.
For each, ask who is doing the -ing and check whether it is the subject of the main clause.
Mark any that dangle.
Then note where you found them.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: participle clauses are common in written English and rare in speech, which is why they feel formal. Instructions and reports use them heavily.
The second finding is that at least one of six usually dangles, and it is almost always in professional writing rather than in anything careless. The reason is that the writer knows who they meant, so the sentence reads correctly to them.
Having completed the form, it should be returned to reception is the classic shape — the form did not complete itself. You will find something very close to that within a page or two of most official instructions, and once you have seen one you will not stop seeing them.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. had already left — NEEDED (already signals an earlier past)
2. finished / sent — NOT NEEDED (the order is obvious)
3. had already come — NEEDED (by the time)
4. had moved — NEEDED (before I arrived, and the reader meets it later)
5. had noticed / had mentioned — NEEDED if this is being introduced as earlier background; NOT NEEDED if the sequence is already established
6. had been waiting — NEEDED, and continuous
7. had / left — NOT NEEDED (a plain sequence)
8. had been — NEEDED (this is the earliest event and it is told last)
9. checked / signed — NOT NEEDED (obvious order)
10. had disappeared — NEEDED (by the time)
11. had not been told — NEEDED (it explains something that came after)
12. opened / went — NOT NEEDED
The NEEDED ones cluster around three signals: already, by the time, and before. Where none of those appears and the order is obvious, the past simple is better.
Number 5 has two defensible answers, which is worth noticing — the tense depends on how you have framed the paragraph, not only on the events.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Walking home, I realised I had left my keys.
2. Having finished the report, I went home.
3. Having checked it twice, she signed it.
4. Turning round, I saw him arriving.
5. Not having been told, he carried on working.
6. Standing at the edge, she saw the whole thing.
7. Having read the file, I understood the problem.
8. Waiting for the part, they started something else.
9. Having already apologised, she said nothing further.
10. Opening the door, I noticed the smell.
11. Having worked there for a decade, he knew everybody.
12. Having checked the loading, I moved the trolley. (or: the supervisor moved the trolley)
The -ing versions — 1, 4, 6, 8, 10 — are all simultaneous or immediately linked. The having versions — 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 — are all completed before the main clause.
Number 5 puts not before having, which is the standard position for the negative.
Number 12 was a dangling participle: the original says the trolley did the checking. Every one of your answers should survive the test — ask who is doing the -ing, and check it is the subject of what follows.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — it is your account.
What most people find: at least one past perfect is unnecessary, and it is usually in the first half. Learners who have just learned the tense apply it to the first thing that happened in the account, when the past simple would do — the reader has no earlier past to be confused about yet.
The second finding is the opposite and it is more useful. There is often one place where a past perfect is missing, and it is where the writer introduced something the reader had not been told about. That is exactly where the tense earns its place, and it is the hardest spot to notice yourself because you already knew the information.
Giving it to somebody else finds that spot faster than anything else.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key.
What most people find: participle clauses are common in written English and rare in speech, which is why they feel formal. Instructions and reports use them heavily.
The second finding is that at least one of six usually dangles, and it is almost always in professional writing rather than in anything careless. The reason is that the writer knows who they meant, so the sentence reads correctly to them.
Having completed the form, it should be returned to reception is the classic shape — the form did not complete itself. You will find something very close to that within a page or two of most official instructions, and once you have seen one you will not stop seeing them.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Both were giving the setting before the event — Checking the loading sheet and walking through Bay 2 were both already under way when the stack fell, which is exactly what the past continuous marks.
